clue.text: Grammatical fluency largely acquired by male poet

indicators.note: acquired by says the word for male takes in the shortened word

parts.note: he is the male pronoun

indicators.note: largely means most of the word, so its last letter goes

parts.note: oracy is fluency and correctness in spoken language

explanation.surface: A man of verse is praised for picking up most of a polished way with words.
explanation.walkthrough: Oracy is a schoolroom term for skill in speaking, rarely met outside education. 'male' sits beside 'poet' as if describing it, but supplies letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Horace was a celebrated Roman lyric poet, author of the Odes, so he is an example of a poet.

clue.text: Plan Chad devised, getting reluctant applause?

indicators.note: devised means worked out or reorganised, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A plan drawn up by Chad earns only grudging applause.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that the definition is loose: a slow handclap is the grudging or impatient kind of clapping.
explanation.definitionFit: A handclap is a single clap of the hands, and a slow one signals grudging, unwilling applause.

clue.text: Soldier's condition, last to fall in Marne battle

indicators.note: in says these letters go inside the rearranged battle name
battle signals that the letters of Marne fight it out into a new order

parts.note: if introduces a condition

indicators.note: last to points to the final letter of the word fall

explanation.surface: A soldier's state as the last man falls in the Battle of the Marne.
explanation.walkthrough: 'battle' shuffles the river name to REMAN, and 'in' puts the condition word plus the end of 'fall' after its first letter. The Marne was a First World War battle; here it is only letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A rifleman is an infantry soldier armed with a rifle, or a private in a rifle regiment.

clue.text: Cambridge college academic welcomes northern historian

indicators.note: welcomes means takes in, so the college and academic words enclose the letter

parts.note: Clare is a college of Cambridge University
a don is a university teacher

explanation.surface: A Cambridge college lecturer greets a northern historian.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter goes between the two words, the college and the academic, rather than inside either. Edward Hyde, Earl of Clarendon, wrote a history of the English Civil War.
explanation.definitionFit: The first Earl of Clarendon wrote The History of the Rebellion, so he is famous as a historian.

clue.text: One Greek couple touring Germany went to live elsewhere

indicators.note: touring means going all round, so the word for couple surrounds the other letters

parts.note: to couple is to pair or mate
one is the Roman numeral I
D is the international vehicle code for Germany (Deutschland)

explanation.surface: A Greek pair travel round Germany and end up moving abroad.
explanation.walkthrough: 'touring Germany' reads as one phrase, but 'touring' works on the earlier pieces and Germany is simply tacked on at the end.
explanation.definitionFit: To migrate is to move from one region to settle in another, which is going to live elsewhere.

clue.text: Part of Vermeer's self-introduction? That can't be true

definitions.meaning: the painter Vermeer came from Delft, so introducing himself he might mention his nationality
a British idiom of disbelief, as in 'if that's true, I'm a ...'

explanation.surface: An imagined greeting from the Dutch painter, met with disbelief.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom says a claim is so unlikely that, if it were true, the speaker would be from the Netherlands.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase is a stock expression of scepticism, and also literally what the Delft painter could say of his nationality.

clue.text: 15 perhaps and cattle thief? No way

definitions.note: the title character of the play at 15-down is an ancient British monarch, an example of a sovereign

indicators.note: No says the letters for way are absent from the thief word

parts.note: a rustler steals livestock
St is the abbreviation for street, a way

explanation.surface: A cattle thief claims to be a king, and the reply is no way.
explanation.walkthrough: 'No' removes ST from RUSTLER. 'No way' reads as an exclamation, but 'No' is the deletion and 'way' the letters removed.
explanation.definitionFit: The character at 15 is a king, and a king is an example of someone who governs a realm.

clue.text: Work about sixty minutes? That's exciting

indicators.note: about says the soil-working word goes around the hour

parts.note: to till is to work the soil
hr is the abbreviation for hour

explanation.surface: Working for an hour or so turns out to be thrilling.
explanation.definitionFit: A thrill is a sudden surge of excitement, so something that gives one is exciting; the definition is a phrase used loosely.

clue.text: Plan to remove roadside assistance?

definitions.meaning: read as ..., to take away the road signs that help drivers

explanation.surface: A scheme to scrap the breakdown recovery service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'roadside assistance' suggests breakdown services; here it means road signs, and the prefix de- takes them away.
explanation.definitionFit: A design is a plan or drawing made before something is built, and to design is to plan.

clue.text: What those cured of phobias have? Definitely not

definitions.text: What those cured of phobias have?
definitions.meaning: people rid of their phobias are left without fright
the exclamation used as an emphatic refusal, like 'not a chance!'

explanation.surface: A quip about what therapy leaves behind, answered with a flat refusal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone cured of phobias has no fright left; and the colloquial exclamation means certainly not.

clue.text: In hospital rooms look after last of our great fighters

indicators.note: In says the following letters go inside the hospital rooms word

parts.note: wards are rooms in a hospital

indicators.note: after says the word for look comes behind the final letter of our
last of picks the final letter of the word our

parts.note: lo is an old word meaning look or behold

explanation.surface: Hospital wards tending the last of our great warriors.
explanation.walkthrough: 'look after' reads as caring for patients, but splits: 'look' gives letters and 'after' sets their order.
explanation.definitionFit: Warlords are military commanders, powerful fighting leaders, so great fighters is a fair loose description.

clue.text: French snack rejected by Lance Percival

indicators.note: rejected says the hidden letters are read backwards
the clue word that says the letters sit inside the next words

parts.note: the letters run across the end of one word into the next

explanation.surface: The comic actor Lance Percival turns down a French nibble.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters EPERC sit across 'lancE PERCival', and 'rejected' turns them round. Lance Percival was a British comedy actor and calypso singer.
explanation.definitionFit: A crêpe is a thin French pancake, often eaten as a light snack from street stalls.

clue.text: Cricketer out, say, after half a century

indicators.note: after says the abbreviation for say follows the numeral

parts.note: out of fashion, so square or uncool
a century is 100, half is 50, the Roman numeral L
say means for example, abbreviated eg

explanation.surface: A batsman is dismissed just after reaching his fifty.
explanation.walkthrough: Square leg is a fielding position in cricket, level with the batsman on the leg side, and by extension the fielder there. 'Cricketer out' looks like a dismissal, but 'out' is SQUARE.
explanation.definitionFit: Fielders are named by their positions, so the player at square leg is a cricketer.

clue.text: Preachy nun sees to it in new order

indicators.note: in new order says these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A sanctimonious nun takes charge of things in a new religious order.
explanation.walkthrough: 'new order' looks like a religious community, a natural home for a nun, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Sententious means given to pompous moralising, which is to be preachy.

clue.text: About to enter badly vandalised treasure store

indicators.note: to enter says the letters for about go inside the rearranged word
badly says the letters of vandalised are jumbled

parts.note: ca, short for circa, means about

explanation.surface: A treasure hoard has been badly vandalised by someone getting in.
explanation.walkthrough: Aladdin's cave, from the Arabian Nights tale, is a byword for a place full of riches.
explanation.definitionFit: The phrase describes any place crammed with valuables, from the hoard in the folk tale, so it names a treasure store.

clue.text: Imagine one suit half-packed in case

indicators.note: packed in says these letters go inside the luggage word

parts.note: a valise is a small travelling case
one is the Roman numeral I

indicators.note: half says only the first two of the four letters of suit are used

explanation.surface: Picture one suit, half packed, sitting in a suitcase.
explanation.walkthrough: 'half-packed' is one word in the surface but two jobs: 'half' trims the suit, 'packed in' does the enclosing.
explanation.definitionFit: To visualise is to form a mental picture of something, which is to imagine it.

clue.text: Play, breaking a leg in park after dad leaves

indicators.note: breaking says the letters are smashed into a new order
leaves says the word for dad goes out of park

parts.note: pa is a word for dad

explanation.surface: An actor in an outdoor play breaks a leg in the park after his father walks out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'leaves' takes PA from PARK, leaving RK; 'breaking' shuffles A LEG IN with RK. 'Break a leg' is theatre slang for good luck.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a tragedy by Shakespeare, so it is an example of a stage play.

clue.text: An English church's attempt to identify forefathers?

parts.note: CE is the Church of England, and the 's adds S
a try is an attempt

explanation.surface: An Anglican church's efforts at tracing family history.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is a plural noun standing for a collective one: a person's forefathers taken together are their lineage.
explanation.definitionFit: Ancestry means one's line of descent, and by extension the ancestors themselves taken together.

clue.text: Stop to do burials near church

parts.note: to inter is to bury a body
a mission is a church or chapel set up by missionaries

explanation.surface: An instruction to halt burials close to the church.
explanation.definitionFit: An intermission is a pause or break, such as the interval in a performance, so it is a stop.

clue.text: Sergeant major with weapons speaks ingratiatingly

parts.note: arms are weapons

explanation.surface: An armed sergeant major sweet-talks his way along.
explanation.definitionFit: To smarm is to flatter in an oily, insincere way, which is to speak ingratiatingly.

clue.text: Hot garment made of fur, perhaps, new

parts.note: a stole is a wrap worn round the shoulders, often of fur

explanation.surface: A brand-new fur garment, hot off the rack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hot' looks like a temperature, but it is slang for taken illegally.
explanation.definitionFit: Hot is slang for stolen goods, recently taken and so risky to handle.

clue.text: Shabby playhouse right to be got rid of within twenty-four hours

indicators.note: within says the shortened playhouse word goes inside the day

parts.note: a day, here Mon, short for Monday

indicators.note: to be got rid of says the letter for right is removed from the playhouse word

parts.note: a playhouse is a theatre

explanation.surface: A shabby old theatre is cleared out in a single day.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to be got rid of' leaves THEATE once the right letter goes, and 'within' sets that inside the short day name.
explanation.definitionFit: Clothes eaten by moths are full of holes, hence worn and shabby in general use.

clue.text: Gain access to part of hospital — emergency room

parts.note: ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: Getting into a hospital through the emergency room.
explanation.definitionFit: To enter a place is to go into it, which is to gain access.

clue.text: Contend a miscreant has nothing to lose

indicators.note: to lose says the letter for nothing is dropped from the word for miscreant

parts.note: a rogue is a scoundrel or wrongdoer
O is the figure zero, nothing

explanation.surface: Someone claims a wrongdoer has nothing to lose.
explanation.definitionFit: To contend is to assert or maintain a point in debate, the same as to argue.

clue.text: Family member, for example, avoids demotion

indicators.note: avoids says the abbreviation is missing from the demotion word

parts.note: relegation is demotion, as of a team to a lower division

explanation.surface: A relative, for example, escapes being demoted at work.
explanation.walkthrough: 'avoids' removes EG from RELEGATION. 'for example' looks like a link to the definition, but it supplies the letters.
explanation.definitionFit: A relation is a relative, someone connected by blood or marriage.

clue.text: Most pleasant, having temperature just above freezing in home

indicators.note: in says the temperature goes inside the word for home

parts.note: a nest is a home, as for a bird
one degree Celsius, written 1C, is just over the freezing point of water

explanation.surface: The cosiest home is one kept a touch above freezing.
explanation.walkthrough: One degree Celsius, written 1C, is read as the letters I and C.
explanation.definitionFit: Nice means agreeable, so its superlative is the most agreeable or pleasant.

clue.text: Garment made of lightweight material, small strip

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
to strip is to undress

explanation.surface: A short strip of light fabric becomes a summer outfit.
explanation.definitionFit: A sundress is a light, often sleeveless dress worn in hot weather, cut from thin fabric.

clue.text: The old railway crosses area every so often

indicators.note: crosses says the old words go over and around the letter for area

parts.note: ye is an old form of the, as in Ye Olde Shoppe

explanation.surface: An old-fashioned railway line passes through a district now and then.
explanation.walkthrough: The letter for area sits between the two pieces, not inside either.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done once a year happens at regular intervals, so the loose sense of periodically fits.
